You are the coordinator of /acs:create-prd. You produce or amend the PRD doc set in
the consumer repo — wherever the repo already keeps its PRD, else at
`docs/product/`: the hub `prd.md` and one PRD per feature at
`features/<slug>/prd.md` (ADR-0142) — as a **ticketless run**, and you leave the documents as uncommitted changes in the working tree:
no ticket, no branch, no commit, no PR (ADR-0127). `/acs:create-pr`, given a
prompt (e.g. `/acs:create-pr "Amend the PRD: cut order tracking"`), commits them
and opens the PR when the user is ready. You never write `roadmap.md`: the
roadmap that schedules these features is `/acs:manage-roadmap`'s (ADR-0145),
and a run that changes the feature set points the user at it.
You orchestrate three subagents — surveyor → authors → review: a read-only
surveyor establishes the mode, the outline, the feature set and the open
questions, you put the questions to the user, authors write the documents from
the notes and the answers, and a reviewer judges them fresh. You never write
the PRD content yourself. Every phase fans out: the survey runs as parallel
surveyor slices over disjoint areas of the repo when a brownfield or amend code
survey spans two or more of them, the write runs the `hub` author first and then
one author per feature in parallel, and the review always runs as two parallel
reviewer slices over disjoint check dimensions, beside the deterministic floor
you run yourself.

MANDATORY first action. Locate the repo's PRD the way any session finds a
document: CLAUDE.md and whatever docs index it or the repo points at (e.g.
`docs/README.md`), then a Glob/Grep for `prd.md` or a PRD by content. Found →
this is an **amend** run; that file is `<prd>`. Not found → ask acs where the
PRD folder is — `python3 "/home/user/gms-marketplace/plugins/acs/hooks/scripts/acs.py" docs where
--doc living:prd` — and `<prd>` = `<path>/prd.md`. The PRD is a living document, always shared, but acs never
creates a new docs folder without asking (ADR-0132): when `needs` names
`location` (`location_source: default` — no `docs.prd_dir` setting, no existing
folder), the folder is a question in the ONE grouped ask (User interaction) —
use `proposed_path` (e.g. `docs/product`) or give another repo-relative folder,
no keep-local option — saved for the team with `acs.py docs decide --location
prd=<folder>`; until then the author writes nothing there. This mirrors the
surveyor's amend definition (see Survey below). Then run exactly:

python3 "/home/user/gms-marketplace/plugins/acs/hooks/scripts/acs.py" step start --step create-prd --args "Treat everything below as confirmed; do not ask the user anything.

If `context.reconcile` is true, or `context.handoff_summary` exists, read

## Reflection loop — surveyor → author → review

The loop is surveyor → author → review, max 3 iterations. Iteration 1 runs
the surveyor once: it classifies the mode, surveys the codebase or plans the
elicitation, and writes the authoring notes (the outline, the feature set, the open
questions, the two corroboration sections the review's deterministic floor parses)

reviewer judges the result fresh. On iterations 2-3 the reviewer's findings go
verbatim into the next author `<task>` `<context>` — each to the author that owns
the file — and the authors author the remediation — the surveyor never runs again;
its notes are the fixed baseline every later iteration is judged against.

authors are one round). The survey belongs
to iteration 1 and is not a round of its own. `/acs:create-prd` has no
path-driven review-depth selection: the cap is a fixed 3 on every run.

the namespaced one). Spawn each role under the name in `context.agents.<role>` — the plugin's
`acs:create-prd-<role>`, or the generated `acs-create-prd-<role>` copy

first spawn: the foreground rule, the message check, what is persisted at each
phase boundary, and the fan-out rules (slice ids, slice plans, the join, the
cap) every sliced phase follows.

The surveyor's first job is mode classification:

  features (MoSCoW), product NFRs, constraints, out-of-scope.

The surveyor also runs the shared ADR-0012 design-time doc-consistency step;
any findings surface through the "Clarification ledger first" mechanism below

classification, the outline, the open questions and the two corroboration
sections in its authoring notes and returns `needs_input` with the open

Each author completes the `## Answer fidelity` anchors against the text it
wrote. Should one return `needs_input` (a product fact the answers do not
settle), ask the user and re-run that author for the same iteration with the
answer in `<context>`.

**The hub is one author, and runs first.** The hub's Features index is the
seam every feature PRD hangs from (its title, MoSCoW group and goals), so it is
settled before any feature is written. The feature PRDs are disjoint, derive from the hub's index and run in

### Versions — after every author result (ADR-0122, ADR-0130)

Every document of the set — `prd.md` and each feature's `prd.md` — is
versioned: it opens with the front-matter block (`status`, `version`,

the first author spawn and after every author result: what to record where the
run started, and when each file's block is initialised, bumped or left alone.
A feature a run does not touch keeps its version.

document of the set and the git diff) — never the author's reasoning. Its

and the review — its slices plus the floor you run — checks, all findings
blocking:

- all eight required `prd.md` sections present and non-empty, and every
  feature PRD with its six sections; the Features index and the
  documents agree (each Must/Should/Could feature links an existing document,
  none is unlinked);
- every feature traces to at least one goal, in the hub's bullet and in its own

- every goal has at least one **measurable** success metric (value + unit +

- nothing in features or NFRs contradicts the stated constraints or the
  out-of-scope list;
- amend mode: `git diff` shows only the intended sections changed — the
  leading front-matter block aside, which must show the version bumped (the
  version `versions-before.json` recorded + 1, status `proposed`);
- every document carries a valid version front-matter block (`acs.py design check`).

Read `/home/user/gms-marketplace/plugins/acs/skills/create-prd/references/review-slices.md`

repo-relative, in result `states.files`. The final message lists those files and
points the user at `/acs:create-pr "<what the PRD change is>"` (e.g.

# /acs:create-prd — spawning, messages and the fan-out

Open this before the first spawn of a run and keep to it for every phase
after: how an agent is spawned and waited on, how its messages are checked
and persisted, and the rules every sliced phase follows.

**Spawn in the foreground and wait on the result, never on a clock.** Pass
`run_in_background: false` to the Agent tool: the phase's `<result>` is your
next input and nothing else can usefully happen while it runs. If the
runtime moves the agent to the background anyway, wait for its completion
notification — never poll with `sleep` loops (`for i in $(seq 1 40); do
sleep 15; done` and its kin), which wait a fixed ten minutes whatever the
agent did and spent a whole 1800s setup on the 2026-09-15 release gate.

All messages follow `the SubagentStop hook's message check`; the `phase=` of
every task and result is the role (`surveyor`, `author`, `reviewer`). On an
invalid message, re-request it once; if still invalid, fail the run with the
validation error recorded in `errors`.

Every phase output is persisted at the phase boundary, BEFORE the next phase
starts: the SubagentStop hook snapshots each returned message to
`steps/create-prd/iter-<n>/<role>-message.xml`; if that snapshot is missing (a
host that does not fire the hook), write the `<task>` and `<result>` there
yourself. The roles' own artifacts are the authoring notes
`iter-<n>/authoring.md` (Mode & evidence; PRD outline; Feature set; Code
evidence; Answer fidelity; Open questions; Risks; Reviewer checklist — the surveyor writes iteration 1's, the author completes them and
carries them forward), `iter-1/surveyor.json`, `iter-<n>/author-hub.json` and
`iter-<n>/author-feature-<slug>.json` (the author is always sliced:
`author-slices.md`), each feature author's `features/<slug>/notes.md` and
`iter-<n>/reviewer.md`; every iteration's reviewer `<inputs>` name that
iteration's authoring notes. Decomposition is YOURS alone — subagents never
spawn subagents.

### Fan-out — slices, the join, the cap

Every fan-out in this skill is yours: you spawn N instances of the SAME agent
in ONE message (all foreground, all in the same Agent-tool batch), wait for
ALL of them, and join their outputs before the next phase starts. The rules
every sliced phase follows:

- **Slice id on the wire.** Each parallel instance's `<task>` carries
  `slice="<id>"` (`<task skill="create-prd" phase="reviewer" slice="delta" …>`)
  and its `<result>` echoes it, so the SubagentStop snapshot lands at
  `iter-<n>/<role>-<id>-message.xml` with no collision. An un-sliced instance
  omits `slice` exactly as before. A slice id is a short lowercase name
  (`api`, `web-app`, `delta`); the join derives each id from the part of the
  file name after the prefix all its inputs share, so ids may carry hyphens.
- **Slice plan first.** Before spawning, write (through `acs.py write`) the partition to
  `steps/create-prd/iter-<n>/<role>-slices.json` (`{"<id>": [<the paths or
  dimension numbers it owns>], …}`), so a resume knows which slices were
  planned. The author's plan lists the feature wave only — written once the
  `hub` has returned (`author-slices.md`); the `hub` is evidenced by its own
  report.
- **Per-slice files.** A surveyor slice writes `iter-1/authoring-<id>.md` and
  `iter-1/surveyor-<id>.json`; an author slice writes `iter-<n>/author-<id>.json`
  (a feature author also its `features/<slug>/notes.md`); a reviewer slice
  writes `iter-<n>/reviewer-<id>.md`.
- **The join is deterministic, never prose-merging by you.** One command joins
  the slice files by `## ` heading (first file's preamble; each H2 once, in
  first-seen order; bodies concatenated in input order, each prefixed by a
  `<!-- slice: <id> -->` line) into the ONE file every downstream reader and
  checker reads:

  ```bash
  python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/acs.py" notes merge \
    --out <partition>/steps/create-prd/iter-<n>/<joined file> \
    <partition>/steps/create-prd/iter-<n>/<slice file 1> <…slice file 2> …
  ```

  It prints `{ok, out, sections, inputs}` and refuses when a slice file is
  missing — a missing slice is a failed slice, never a smaller join.
- **Cap.** At most `settings.parallel.max_agents` (default 4) instances per
  message; beyond the cap, run the slices in waves of that size (each wave one
  message) and join once after the last wave.

# /acs:create-prd — the PRD doc set (ADR-0142)

The PRD is a **hub plus one PRD per feature**, the layout product teams use to
keep a PRD reviewable as it grows: the hub holds what is true of the whole
product, each feature's document holds what is true of that feature, and ids
link the two. The author, the reviewer and the floor all work from this page.

```
<prd_dir>/                       (wherever the repo keeps its PRD, else docs/product/)
  prd.md                         the hub — the product PRD
  roadmap.md                     milestones → release versions — /acs:manage-roadmap's, never this skill (ADR-0145)
  features/<slug>/prd.md         one PRD per feature (a Won't-have feature may have none)
  features/<slug>/analysis/      the feature's living analysis — /acs:analyze-requirements, never this skill
```

`<slug>` is the kebab-case feature slug the rest of acs already uses
(`lld/<slug>/`, a ticket's `features`), so one name reaches the feature's PRD,
analysis, LLD and tickets.

## The hub — `prd.md`

EXACTLY the `required_sections`, in order, each non-empty: the `## ` headings
of the hub template (`acs.py prd template`, ADR-0147) — the repo's
`.acs/templates/prd-default.md`, else the built-in, whose eight are **Vision**,
**Problem statement**, **Target users & personas**, **Goals & success
metrics**, **Features (prioritized)**, **Non-functional requirements**,
**Constraints & assumptions**, **Out of scope**. A new hub starts from the
template: its title and headings in order, each section written to the
template's guidance comment; the comments are not kept. **Features
(prioritized)** is the *index*:

- `### Must have`, `### Should have`, `### Could have`, `### Won't have` groups;
  every feature one top-level bullet, in exactly one group:

  ```
  - [Wishlist](features/wishlist/prd.md) — save products for later (supports G1, G3)
  ```

  The link is the feature's PRD; `(supports G<n>, …)` names the goal ids it
  serves, the ids defined in **Goals & success metrics** (`G1: …`). A
  Won't-have bullet may omit the link and carries its reason instead.
- A goal no feature serves gets an explicit deferral note in the index.
- The hub never restates a feature's requirements — it links them.
- **Non-functional requirements** are the product-wide ones; a feature's own
  performance or accessibility bar lives in that feature's PRD.

## A feature PRD — `features/<slug>/prd.md`

EXACTLY the `feature_required_sections`, in order, each non-empty — the `## `
headings of the feature template (`.acs/templates/prd-feature-default.md`,
else the built-in, whose six are below) — starting from the template like the
hub; the document opens at its `# <Feature name>` title. A repo template may add
sections or rename others, never drop **Goals served** or **Requirements**
(`acs.py prd template` refuses one that does: tickets link `R<n>` ids, ADR-0144,
and the implemented status is derived from them, ADR-0146):

| Section | Holds |
|---|---|
| **Summary** | what the feature is and the user problem it answers, in a paragraph |
| **Goals served** | the goal ids the hub's bullet names — the same set, each with how this feature moves its metric |
| **Requirements** | one line per requirement: `- **R1** — <the capability, observable and testable>`. Ids are `R<n>`, unique in the document, never reused or renumbered when one is cut (cite them as `<slug>/R1`) |
| **Acceptance criteria** | the feature-level done-when: concrete, testable statements (Given/When/Then or measurable thresholds) that trace to the requirement ids |
| **Dependencies** | other features (by slug), systems or decisions it needs; `None.` when there are none |
| **Out of scope** | what this feature deliberately does not do |

Priority is NOT a section: the hub's MoSCoW group is its one source, so the two
cannot drift. A feature-specific NFR is a requirement (`R<n>`) with a measurable
threshold.

## What the floor checks

`prd_feature_check.py` (rules in its docstring) holds the layout deterministically:
every Must/Should/Could bullet links a document, every link resolves, every
document is linked, the goal ids agree between the hub's bullet and the
feature's **Goals served** (and exist), the sections are present, in order and
non-empty, and the requirement ids are present and unique. Whether a requirement
is really testable, and an acceptance criterion really traces to it, is the
`substance` reviewer's judgement.

## Amend mode

The hub is edited in place, untouched sections byte-for-byte. A feature the
amendment does not touch keeps its document untouched (so its version is not
bumped). A new feature gets a new document. A **cut** feature moves to **Won't
have** keeping its link; nothing deletes a feature PRD — retiring it is
`/acs:set-doc-status deprecated`, a person's call.

## Versions

Every document of the set — the hub and each feature PRD — carries
the version front matter, set only by the coordinator through `acs.py design`
(see `versions.md`); an author never writes it.
# /acs:create-prd — the author: the hub first, then one writer per feature

Open this at Author, every iteration. The document shapes are `documents.md`;
the slice ids, the cap and the plan file are `fan-out.md`. Author spawns are
`acs:create-prd-author` with `phase="author"` and a `slice`.

## The two kinds of author slice

| Slice | Owns (and writes nothing else) | Runs |
|---|---|---|
| `hub` | `<prd>`, `iter-<n>/authoring.md` | first, alone |
| `feature-<slug>` | `<prd_dir>/features/<slug>/prd.md` and `steps/create-prd/features/<slug>/notes.md` | after `hub`, every one together in ONE message |

**Why this partition.** The hub is one document whose Features index every
other document hangs from, so it is ONE writer; nothing can own half of it.
(The roadmap that schedules the features is `/acs:manage-roadmap`'s, ADR-0145.)
The feature PRDs, by contrast, are disjoint files that each derive
from the hub's **Features (prioritized)** entry for their slug (title, MoSCoW
group, goals served), so they cannot be written until the hub has settled that
index, and once it has they cannot collide. The hub also owns the synthesis of a
sliced survey (`survey-slices.md`) and the notes' `## Feature set`: the final
list of slugs, titles, groups and goals the feature writers are cut from.

## The sequence, per iteration

1. **Hub.** Spawn one `hub` author with the notes, the answers and — from
   iteration 2 — the findings whose `file` is the hub or the notes.
   It writes `<prd>`, finalizes `## Feature set` and completes
   the notes' lines that anchor in `prd.md`, and reports in
   `iter-<n>/author-hub.json` the slugs whose documents must be (re)written:
   `features_to_write` — every feature on iteration 1; later, each one it added,
   renamed, re-prioritised or re-pointed at other goals, beside the ones the
   findings name. A feature the hub did not touch and no finding names is not
   re-run, and its document is not bumped.
2. **Plan the wave.** From `features_to_write` plus the features the findings

`file`: a feature PRD → that feature's slice; the hub, a finding
about the feature set or one without a file → `hub`. A finding the hub's fix
turns into a change of the index is picked up by `features_to_write`.

## The notes and the floor

The notes stay ONE file per iteration, `iter-<n>/authoring.md`, owned by the
hub: the surveyor's lines naming a feature PRD as their target
(`- C-3 — features/wishlist/prd.md — …`) are placeholders the hub leaves
alone. The floor reads each feature's notes beside it (`--feature-notes`), and
a feature author's line for a ledger id wins over the placeholder, so a re-run
feature replaces only its own lines and nothing is joined by hand.

## Amend mode

`git diff` discipline spans the whole set (`git diff -- "<prd>"
"<prd_dir>/features"` plus `git status --short -- "<prd_dir>"` for the new
documents). A feature slice edits its existing document in place, preserving
untouched sections byte-for-byte; a new feature's slice creates its document.

once, and if it fails again the iteration counts as failed with its error as a

# /acs:create-prd — the PRD doc set (ADR-0142)

The PRD is a **hub plus one PRD per feature**, the layout product teams use to
keep a PRD reviewable as it grows: the hub holds what is true of the whole
product, each feature's document holds what is true of that feature, and ids
link the two. The author, the reviewer and the floor all work from this page.

```
<prd_dir>/                       (wherever the repo keeps its PRD, else docs/product/)
  prd.md                         the hub — the product PRD
  roadmap.md                     milestones → release versions — /acs:manage-roadmap's, never this skill (ADR-0145)
  features/<slug>/prd.md         one PRD per feature (a Won't-have feature may have none)
  features/<slug>/analysis/      the feature's living analysis — /acs:analyze-requirements, never this skill
```

`<slug>` is the kebab-case feature slug the rest of acs already uses
(`lld/<slug>/`, a ticket's `features`), so one name reaches the feature's PRD,
analysis, LLD and tickets.

## The hub — `prd.md`

EXACTLY the `required_sections`, in order, each non-empty: the `## ` headings
of the hub template (`acs.py prd template`, ADR-0147) — the repo's
`.acs/templates/prd-default.md`, else the built-in, whose eight are **Vision**,
**Problem statement**, **Target users & personas**, **Goals & success
metrics**, **Features (prioritized)**, **Non-functional requirements**,
**Constraints & assumptions**, **Out of scope**. A new hub starts from the
template: its title and headings in order, each section written to the
template's guidance comment; the comments are not kept. **Features
(prioritized)** is the *index*:

- `### Must have`, `### Should have`, `### Could have`, `### Won't have` groups;
  every feature one top-level bullet, in exactly one group:

  ```
  - [Wishlist](features/wishlist/prd.md) — save products for later (supports G1, G3)
  ```

  The link is the feature's PRD; `(supports G<n>, …)` names the goal ids it
  serves, the ids defined in **Goals & success metrics** (`G1: …`). A
  Won't-have bullet may omit the link and carries its reason instead.
- A goal no feature serves gets an explicit deferral note in the index.
- The hub never restates a feature's requirements — it links them.
- **Non-functional requirements** are the product-wide ones; a feature's own
  performance or accessibility bar lives in that feature's PRD.

## A feature PRD — `features/<slug>/prd.md`

EXACTLY the `feature_required_sections`, in order, each non-empty — the `## `
headings of the feature template (`.acs/templates/prd-feature-default.md`,
else the built-in, whose six are below) — starting from the template like the
hub; the document opens at its `# <Feature name>` title. A repo template may add
sections or rename others, never drop **Goals served** or **Requirements**
(`acs.py prd template` refuses one that does: tickets link `R<n>` ids, ADR-0144,
and the implemented status is derived from them, ADR-0146):

| Section | Holds |
|---|---|
| **Summary** | what the feature is and the user problem it answers, in a paragraph |
| **Goals served** | the goal ids the hub's bullet names — the same set, each with how this feature moves its metric |
| **Requirements** | one line per requirement: `- **R1** — <the capability, observable and testable>`. Ids are `R<n>`, unique in the document, never reused or renumbered when one is cut (cite them as `<slug>/R1`) |
| **Acceptance criteria** | the feature-level done-when: concrete, testable statements (Given/When/Then or measurable thresholds) that trace to the requirement ids |
| **Dependencies** | other features (by slug), systems or decisions it needs; `None.` when there are none |
| **Out of scope** | what this feature deliberately does not do |

Priority is NOT a section: the hub's MoSCoW group is its one source, so the two
cannot drift. A feature-specific NFR is a requirement (`R<n>`) with a measurable
threshold.

## What the floor checks

`prd_feature_check.py` (rules in its docstring) holds the layout deterministically:
every Must/Should/Could bullet links a document, every link resolves, every
document is linked, the goal ids agree between the hub's bullet and the
feature's **Goals served** (and exist), the sections are present, in order and
non-empty, and the requirement ids are present and unique. Whether a requirement
is really testable, and an acceptance criterion really traces to it, is the
`substance` reviewer's judgement.

## Amend mode

The hub is edited in place, untouched sections byte-for-byte. A feature the
amendment does not touch keeps its document untouched (so its version is not
bumped). A new feature gets a new document. A **cut** feature moves to **Won't
have** keeping its link; nothing deletes a feature PRD — retiring it is

## Versions

Every document of the set — the hub and each feature PRD — carries
the version front matter, set only by the coordinator through `acs.py design`
(see `versions.md`); an author never writes it.

# /acs:create-prd — reviewer slices, the floor, the join and the pass rule

Open this before every review. "Above" below means SKILL.md's Review
section: the reviewer's inputs and constraints, and the checklist the
dimensions (numbered in `create-prd-reviewer.md`) check.

**Reviewer slices and the floor — every iteration, the default.** The review
has eleven check dimensions (numbered in `create-prd-reviewer.md`). The ones a
script settles are not an agent's: **the `floor` is yours**, run with Bash in
the SAME message as the reviewer spawn, as soon as the author has written the
set. The rest run as two slices, each a fresh instance of
`acs:create-prd-reviewer` whose task carries `slice="<id>"` and
`<constraint name="dimensions">` naming the dimension numbers it owns, beside
every input and constraint above:

| Slice | Dimensions | Owns the run of |
|---|---|---|
| `substance` | 2 feature → goal traceability, 3 measurable success metrics, 4 prioritization discipline, 5 constraint consistency, 6 feature index ↔ documents, 7 plan conformance (the semantic ceiling), 11 audience-style | the fresh semantic read of `prd.md` and every feature PRD, and of every entry in the notes' `## Code evidence` and `## Answer fidelity` (the plan's and each feature's notes) sections |
| `delta` | 8 amend-mode diff discipline, 9 iteration 2+ regression check | `git diff` over the whole set (below) and the re-verification of every prior finding |
| `floor` | 1 required sections, 7 plan conformance (the deterministic floor), 10 structure and the version front matter | run by YOU, no agent: `prd_conformance_check.py` (the code-evidence and answer-fidelity check, whose code-evidence family re-opens every citation through the shared citation-check helpers it imports), `structure_lint.py`, `prd_feature_check.py` (the hub's index against the feature PRDs), `acs.py design check` and the heading check — each run here only, exactly once per iteration |

**The floor, in the reviewer's own commands** (dimensions 1, 7 and 10 of
`create-prd-reviewer.md`, which stay the definition):

```bash
grep -n '^#' "<prd>"                               # 1: the eight sections, each non-empty
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/prd_conformance_check.py" \
  --plan <partition>/steps/create-prd/iter-<n>/authoring.md --mode <greenfield|brownfield|amend> \
  --repo-root <repo_root> --clarifications <partition>/clarifications.json \
  --prd "<prd>" \
  [--feature-notes <partition>/steps/create-prd/features/<slug>/notes.md ...]   # one per feature PRD
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/structure_lint.py" \
  --sections "<required_sections, verbatim>" --ordered "<prd>"
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/prd_feature_check.py" \
  --prd "<prd>" --feature-sections "<feature_required_sections, verbatim>"   # 1, 2, 10 for the feature PRDs
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/acs.py" design check "<prd>" \
  $(find "<features_dir>" -name prd.md)   # 10: the version front matter of every document
```

No `--roadmap` and no `--added-heading`: the roadmap is
`/acs:manage-roadmap`'s (ADR-0145). Each stderr `source:line: [rule] message` is one
blocking finding (dimension `Plan conformance`, `traceability` for the
`feature-*` rules of `prd_feature_check.py`, or `structure`); exit 2 is
itself a blocking finding, so a broken invocation never passes. Each problem
`design check` lists, and its `ok: false`, is a blocking finding of dimension
`structure`. Write
`iter-<n>/reviewer-floor.md` (`acs.py write`, as every file below) — one `## ` section per dimension (Required
sections, Plan conformance, Structure) with the exact commands and output,
then `## Findings` — so the join below reads it like a slice's report. The
floor's semantic ceiling (whether the documents actually reflect each recorded
answer, whether a resolved citation substantiates its claim) is not a script's call: the `substance`
slice judges it from the notes' corroboration sections.

Grounding policing applies in every slice. Write `iter-<n>/reviewer-slices.json`
(the two slices; the floor is not a slice), spawn the two slices in ONE message
beside the floor and wait for both. Then **de-duplicate**: the slices and the
floor own disjoint dimensions, so the join below is the synthesis, but two can
still report one defect (a missing section seen by two dimensions). Drop a
finding that cites the same location and the same defect as another slice's
finding, keeping the one with the higher severity, and record every drop —
which finding, from which slice, kept in favour of which — under
`## De-duplicated findings` in `iter-<n>/reviewer-dedup.md` (write `none`
there when nothing was dropped). Join the reports, in the table's order with
the floor between the slices as before, and the de-duplication record last,
into the one report every later reader reads:

```bash
python3 "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/acs.py" notes merge \
  --out <partition>/steps/create-prd/iter-<n>/reviewer.md \
  <partition>/steps/create-prd/iter-<n>/reviewer-substance.md \
  <partition>/steps/create-prd/iter-<n>/reviewer-floor.md \
  <partition>/steps/create-prd/iter-<n>/reviewer-delta.md \
  <partition>/steps/create-prd/iter-<n>/reviewer-dedup.md
```

**Pass rule for sliced reviewers:** the iteration passes only if EVERY slice
returned `status="completed"` with zero blocking findings and the floor found
nothing. Any slice's or the floor's blocking finding blocks the iteration. A slice that failed or returned no usable result
fails the iteration — never "pass with a missing slice"; re-run that slice
once, and if it fails again the iteration counts as failed with its error as a
finding.

# PRD — groomr

## Vision

Every independent dog groomer takes bookings online without phone tag. groomr gives a one- or two-person grooming salon a simple online booking page, automatic reminders and deposits, so pet owners book from their phone and the groomer spends the day grooming rather than answering calls and texts.

## Problem statement

Independent dog groomers lose hours every week to booking by phone and text: answering calls while their hands are busy, chasing replies and juggling the diary by hand. On top of that, no-shows cost them about a fifth of their slots, and an empty slot is income that cannot be recovered. Pet owners, for their part, have to wait for a reply before they know whether a time is free. (The "about a fifth" figure is the brief's own estimate, not measured data; see assumption A2.)

## Target users & personas

- **Groomer** — runs a one- or two-person salon. Sets opening hours and the services on offer. Wants a full diary without phone tag; is frustrated by interruptions during work and by clients who do not turn up.
- **Pet owner** — books and reschedules from a phone. Wants to see free times and book straight away; is frustrated by waiting for a reply and by forgetting appointments.

## Goals & success metrics

| Goal | Metric |
|---|---|
| G1 Groomers take bookings online | 500 bookings a week across all salons combined, by 2027-03-31 |
| G2 Fewer no-shows | No-show rate below 5% of appointments, by 2027-06-30 (from a baseline of about 20% of slots) |

## Features (prioritized)

### Must have

- [Online booking](features/online-booking/prd.md) — pet owners book and reschedule appointments online against the groomer's opening hours and services (supports G1)
- [SMS reminders](features/sms-reminders/prd.md) — the pet owner receives an SMS reminder the day before the appointment (supports G2)

### Should have

- [Deposits at booking](features/deposits/prd.md) — the pet owner pays a deposit when booking, to reduce no-shows (supports G2)

### Could have

- [Loyalty stamp card](features/loyalty-stamp-card/prd.md) — repeat customers collect stamps toward a reward, encouraging return online bookings (supports G1)

### Won't have

- Marketplace ranking groomers against each other — groomr serves each salon's own customers and does not compare salons, which would work against the independent groomers it is built for.

Both goals are served by at least one feature, so no goal is deferred.

## Non-functional requirements

- The booking page loads in under 2 seconds at p95 on a 4G phone.
- The service is available at least 99.5% of each month.

## Constraints & assumptions

Constraints:

- Customers are in the EU only.
- All personal data is stored and processed in an EU region, in line with GDPR.
- SMS messages are sent through a third-party gateway.

Assumptions (to be confirmed or replaced as the product is designed):

- **A1** — The 500 bookings a week in G1 is the total across all salons combined, as the brief states.
- **A2** — The baseline no-show rate of about 20% is the brief's "about a fifth of their slots", an estimate rather than measured data.
- **A3** — The deposit payment method and provider are not yet decided; they are left to design.
- **A4** — The loyalty reward rules (number of stamps, type of reward) are not yet decided; they are left to design.
- **A5** — The SMS gateway is not yet chosen; it must process data in the EU to meet the data constraint above.

## Out of scope

- Native mobile apps; booking is through the web on a phone.
- Payments beyond deposits.
- Marketplace ranking of groomers against each other.

# PRD — groomr

## Vision

Every independent dog groomer takes bookings online without phone tag. groomr gives a one- or two-person grooming salon a simple online booking page, automatic reminders and deposits, so pet owners book from their phone and the groomer spends the day grooming rather than answering calls and texts.

## Problem statement

Independent dog groomers lose hours every week to booking by phone and text: answering calls while their hands are busy, chasing replies and juggling the diary by hand. On top of that, no-shows cost them about a fifth of their slots, and an empty slot is income that cannot be recovered. Pet owners, for their part, have to wait for a reply before they know whether a time is free. (The "about a fifth" figure is the brief's own estimate, not measured data; see assumption A2.)

## Target users & personas

- **Groomer** — runs a one- or two-person salon. Sets opening hours and the services on offer. Wants a full diary without phone tag; is frustrated by interruptions during work and by clients who do not turn up.
- **Pet owner** — books and reschedules from a phone. Wants to see free times and book straight away; is frustrated by waiting for a reply and by forgetting appointments.

## Goals & success metrics

| Goal | Metric |
|---|---|
| G1 Groomers take bookings online | 500 bookings a week across all salons combined, by 2027-03-31 |
| G2 Fewer no-shows | No-show rate below 5% of appointments, by 2027-06-30 (from a baseline of about 20% of slots) |

## Features (prioritized)

### Must have

- [Online booking](features/online-booking/prd.md) — pet owners book and reschedule appointments online against the groomer's opening hours and services (supports G1)
- [SMS reminders](features/sms-reminders/prd.md) — the pet owner receives an SMS reminder the day before the appointment (supports G2)

### Should have

- [Deposits at booking](features/deposits/prd.md) — the pet owner pays a deposit when booking, to reduce no-shows (supports G2)

### Could have

- [Loyalty stamp card](features/loyalty-stamp-card/prd.md) — repeat customers collect stamps toward a reward, encouraging return online bookings (supports G1)

### Won't have

- Marketplace ranking groomers against each other — groomr serves each salon's own customers and does not compare salons, which would work against the independent groomers it is built for.

Both goals are served by at least one feature, so no goal is deferred.

## Non-functional requirements

- The booking page loads in under 2 seconds at p95 on a 4G phone.
- The service is available at least 99.5% of each month.

## Constraints & assumptions

Constraints:

- Customers are in the EU only.
- All personal data is stored and processed in an EU region, in line with GDPR.
- SMS messages are sent through a third-party gateway.

Assumptions (to be confirmed or replaced as the product is designed):

- **A1** — The 500 bookings a week in G1 is the total across all salons combined, as the brief states.
- **A2** — The baseline no-show rate of about 20% is the brief's "about a fifth of their slots", an estimate rather than measured data.
- **A3** — The deposit payment method and provider are not yet decided; they are left to design.
- **A4** — The loyalty reward rules (number of stamps, type of reward) are not yet decided; they are left to design.
- **A5** — The SMS gateway is not yet chosen; it must process data in the EU to meet the data constraint above.

## Out of scope

- Native mobile apps; booking is through the web on a phone.
- Payments beyond deposits.
- Marketplace ranking of groomers against each other.

7	# PRD — groomr
8	
9	## Vision
10	
11	Every independent dog groomer takes bookings online without phone tag. groomr gives a one- or two-person grooming salon a simple online booking page, automatic reminders and deposits, so pet owners book from their phone and the groomer spends the day grooming rather than answering calls and texts.
12	
13	## Problem statement
14	
15	Independent dog groomers lose hours every week to booking by phone and text: answering calls while their hands are busy, chasing replies and juggling the diary by hand. On top of that, no-shows cost them about a fifth of their slots, and an empty slot is income that cannot be recovered. Pet owners, for their part, have to wait for a reply before they know whether a time is free. (The "about a fifth" figure is the brief's own estimate, not measured data; see assumption A2.)
16	
17	## Target users & personas
18	
19	- **Groomer** — runs a one- or two-person salon. Sets opening hours and the services on offer. Wants a full diary without phone tag; is frustrated by interruptions during work and by clients who do not turn up.
20	- **Pet owner** — books and reschedules from a phone. Wants to see free times and book straight away; is frustrated by waiting for a reply and by forgetting appointments.
21	
22	## Goals & success metrics
23	
24	| Goal | Metric |
25	|---|---|
26	| G1 Groomers take bookings online | 500 bookings a week across all salons combined, by 2027-03-31 |
27	| G2 Fewer no-shows | No-show rate below 5% of appointments, by 2027-06-30 (from a baseline of about 20% of slots) |
28	
29	## Features (prioritized)
30	
31	### Must have
32	
33	- [Online booking](features/online-booking/prd.md) — pet owners book and reschedule appointments online against the groomer's opening hours and services (supports G1)
34	- [SMS reminders](features/sms-reminders/prd.md) — the pet owner receives an SMS reminder the day before the appointment (supports G2)
35	
36	### Should have
37	
38	- [Deposits at booking](features/deposits/prd.md) — the pet owner pays a deposit when booking, to reduce no-shows (supports G2)
39	
40	### Could have
41	
42	- [Loyalty stamp card](features/loyalty-stamp-card/prd.md) — repeat customers collect stamps toward a reward, encouraging return online bookings (supports G1)
43	
44	### Won't have
45	
46	- Marketplace ranking groomers against each other — groomr serves each salon's own customers and does not compare salons, which would work against the independent groomers it is built for.
47	
48	Both goals are served by at least one feature, so no goal is deferred.
49	
50	## Non-functional requirements
51	
52	- The booking page loads in under 2 seconds at p95 on a 4G phone.
53	- The service is available at least 99.5% of each month.
54	
55	## Constraints & assumptions
56	
57	Constraints:
58	
59	- Customers are in the EU only.
60	- All personal data is stored and processed in an EU region, in line with GDPR.
61	- SMS messages are sent through a third-party gateway.
62	
63	Assumptions (to be confirmed or replaced as the product is designed):
64	
65	- **A1** — The 500 bookings a week in G1 is the total across all salons combined, as the brief states.
66	- **A2** — The baseline no-show rate of about 20% is the brief's "about a fifth of their slots", an estimate rather than measured data.
67	- **A3** — The deposit payment method and provider are not yet decided; they are left to design.
68	- **A4** — The loyalty reward rules (number of stamps, type of reward) are not yet decided; they are left to design.
69	- **A5** — The SMS gateway is not yet chosen; it must process data in the EU to meet the data constraint above.
70	
71	## Out of scope
72	
73	- Native mobile apps; booking is through the web on a phone.
74	- Payments beyond deposits.
75	- Marketplace ranking of groomers against each other.
76

7	# PRD — groomr
8	
9	## Vision
10	
11	Every independent dog groomer takes bookings online without phone tag. groomr gives a one- or two-person grooming salon a simple online booking page, automatic reminders and deposits, so pet owners book from their phone and the groomer spends the day grooming rather than answering calls and texts.
12	
13	## Problem statement
14	
15	Independent dog groomers lose hours every week to booking by phone and text: answering calls while their hands are busy, chasing replies and juggling the diary by hand. On top of that, no-shows cost them about a fifth of their slots, and an empty slot is income that cannot be recovered. Pet owners, for their part, have to wait for a reply before they know whether a time is free. (The "about a fifth" figure is the brief's own estimate, not measured data; see assumption A2.)
16	
17	## Target users & personas
18	
19	- **Groomer** — runs a one- or two-person salon. Sets opening hours and the services on offer. Wants a full diary without phone tag; is frustrated by interruptions during work and by clients who do not turn up.
20	- **Pet owner** — books and reschedules from a phone. Wants to see free times and book straight away; is frustrated by waiting for a reply and by forgetting appointments.
21	
22	## Goals & success metrics
23	
24	| Goal | Metric |
25	|---|---|
26	| G1 Groomers take bookings online | 500 bookings a week across all salons combined, by 2027-03-31 |
27	| G2 Fewer no-shows | No-show rate below 5% of appointments, by 2027-06-30 (from a baseline of about 20% of slots) |
28	
29	## Features (prioritized)
30	
31	### Must have
32	
33	- [Online booking](features/online-booking/prd.md) — pet owners book and reschedule appointments online against the groomer's opening hours and services (supports G1)
34	- [SMS reminders](features/sms-reminders/prd.md) — the pet owner receives an SMS reminder the day before the appointment (supports G2)
35	
36	### Should have
37	
38	- [Deposits at booking](features/deposits/prd.md) — the pet owner pays a deposit when booking, to reduce no-shows (supports G2)
39	
40	### Could have
41	
42	- [Loyalty stamp card](features/loyalty-stamp-card/prd.md) — repeat customers collect stamps toward a reward, encouraging return online bookings (supports G1)
43	
44	### Won't have
45	
46	- Marketplace ranking groomers against each other — groomr serves each salon's own customers and does not compare salons, which would work against the independent groomers it is built for.
47	
48	Both goals are served by at least one feature, so no goal is deferred.
49	
50	## Non-functional requirements
51	
52	- The booking page loads in under 2 seconds at p95 on a 4G phone.
53	- The service is available at least 99.5% of each month.
54	
55	## Constraints & assumptions
56	
57	Constraints:
58	
59	- Customers are in the EU only.
60	- All personal data is stored and processed in an EU region, in line with GDPR.
61	- SMS messages are sent through a third-party gateway.
62	
63	Assumptions (to be confirmed or replaced as the product is designed):
64	
65	- **A1** — The 500 bookings a week in G1 is the total across all salons combined, as the brief states.
66	- **A2** — The baseline no-show rate of about 20% is the brief's "about a fifth of their slots", an estimate rather than measured data.
67	- **A3** — The deposit payment method and provider are not yet decided; they are left to design.
68	- **A4** — The loyalty reward rules (number of stamps, type of reward) are not yet decided; they are left to design.
69	- **A5** — The SMS gateway is not yet chosen; it must process data in the EU to meet the data constraint above.
70	
71	## Out of scope
72	
73	- Native mobile apps; booking is through the web on a phone.
74	- Payments beyond deposits.
75	- Marketplace ranking of groomers against each other.
76

# Online booking

## Summary

Online booking lets a pet owner book and reschedule a grooming appointment from their phone, choosing from the times a groomer has actually left open. The groomer sets their opening hours and the services they offer, and the booking page works from those. This removes the phone and text back-and-forth that costs independent groomers hours every week, and lets pet owners see a free time and book it straight away.

## Goals served

- G1 — Groomers take bookings online: this feature is how a booking is made, so every booking counted toward the 500 a week by 2027-03-31 goes through it.

## Requirements

- **R1** — A groomer can set their opening hours.
- **R2** — A groomer can set the services they offer.
- **R3** — A pet owner can see the times that are free, based on the groomer's opening hours, the services offered and appointments already booked.
- **R4** — A pet owner can book an appointment for a chosen service in a free time, from a phone browser, without calling or texting the groomer.
- **R5** — A pet owner can reschedule an existing appointment to another free time, from a phone browser.
- **R6** — The same time cannot be booked twice for the same groomer.
- **R7** — The booking page loads in under 2 seconds at p95 on a 4G phone connection.
- **R8** — All personal data collected through booking is stored and processed in an EU region.

## Acceptance criteria

- Given a groomer has set opening hours and services, when a pet owner opens the booking page, then only times inside those hours, for those services, and not already booked are offered (R1, R2, R3).
- Given a free time is offered, when a pet owner books it on a phone, then the appointment is confirmed and appears in the groomer's diary without any call or text (R4).
- Given a pet owner has an appointment, when they reschedule it to another free time on a phone, then the new time is held for them and the old time is offered as free again (R5).
- Given two pet owners try to book the same time for the same groomer, when both submit, then only one booking succeeds and the other is told the time is taken (R6).
- Given page-load measurements of the booking page on a 4G phone connection, when the p95 is calculated over a month, then it is under 2 seconds (R7).
- Given the hosting and storage configuration, when it is inspected, then every store and service that holds booking personal data is in an EU region (R8).

## Dependencies

None.

## Out of scope

- Deposits taken at booking (see the deposits feature).
- SMS reminders (see the sms-reminders feature).
- Loyalty stamps (see the loyalty-stamp-card feature).
- Native mobile apps; booking is through the web on a phone.
EOF

6	
7	# PRD — groomr
8	
9	## Vision
10	
11	Every independent dog groomer takes bookings online without phone tag. groomr gives a one- or two-person grooming salon a simple online booking page, automatic reminders and deposits, so pet owners book from their phone and the groomer spends the day grooming rather than answering calls and texts.
12	
13	## Problem statement
14	
15	Independent dog groomers lose hours every week to booking by phone and text: answering calls while their hands are busy, chasing replies and juggling the diary by hand. On top of that, no-shows cost them about a fifth of their slots, and an empty slot is income that cannot be recovered. Pet owners, for their part, have to wait for a reply before they know whether a time is free. (The "about a fifth" figure is the brief's own estimate, not measured data; see assumption A2.)
16	
17	## Target users & personas
18	
19	- **Groomer** — runs a one- or two-person salon. Sets opening hours and the services on offer. Wants a full diary without phone tag; is frustrated by interruptions during work and by clients who do not turn up.
20	- **Pet owner** — books and reschedules from a phone. Wants to see free times and book straight away; is frustrated by waiting for a reply and by forgetting appointments.
21	
22	## Goals & success metrics
23	
24	| Goal | Metric |
25	|---|---|
26	| G1 Groomers take bookings online | 500 bookings a week across all salons combined, by 2027-03-31 |
27	| G2 Fewer no-shows | No-show rate below 5% of appointments, by 2027-06-30 (from a baseline of about 20% of slots) |
28	
29	## Features (prioritized)
30	
31	### Must have
32	
33	- [Online booking](features/online-booking/prd.md) — pet owners book and reschedule appointments online against the groomer's opening hours and services (supports G1)
34	- [SMS reminders](features/sms-reminders/prd.md) — the pet owner receives an SMS reminder the day before the appointment (supports G2)
35	
36	### Should have
37	
38	- [Deposits at booking](features/deposits/prd.md) — the pet owner pays a deposit when booking, to reduce no-shows (supports G2)
39	
40	### Could have
41	
42	- [Loyalty stamp card](features/loyalty-stamp-card/prd.md) — repeat customers collect stamps toward a reward, encouraging return online bookings (supports G1)
43	
44	### Won't have
45	
46	- Marketplace ranking groomers against each other — groomr serves each salon's own customers and does not compare salons, which would work against the independent groomers it is built for.
47	
48	Both goals are served by at least one feature, so no goal is deferred.
49	
50	## Non-functional requirements
51	
52	- The booking page loads in under 2 seconds at p95 on a 4G phone.
53	- The service is available at least 99.5% of each month.
54	
55	## Constraints & assumptions
56	
57	Constraints:
58

# SMS reminders

## Summary

The pet owner gets a text message the day before their grooming appointment. Owners forget appointments, and every no-show leaves the groomer with an empty slot that cannot be recovered. A reminder sent without any effort from the groomer helps owners turn up, or tell the groomer in good time. The messages go out through a third-party SMS gateway that must process data in an EU region.

## Goals served

- G2 — Fewer no-shows. Reminding the owner the day before the appointment is aimed at bringing the no-show rate below 5% of appointments by 2027-06-30, from a baseline of about 20%.

## Requirements

- **R1** — For every booked appointment, the pet owner receives one SMS reminder on the day before the appointment.
- **R2** — The reminder names the salon and gives the date and time of the appointment.
- **R3** — If an appointment is rescheduled, the reminder follows the new date and time, and no reminder is sent for the old one.
- **R4** — If an appointment is cancelled, no reminder is sent for it.
- **R5** — Reminders are sent through a third-party SMS gateway that processes data in an EU region only (constraint in the hub; assumption A5, the gateway is not yet chosen).
- **R6** — The groomer does not have to do anything for reminders to be sent.

## Acceptance criteria

- Given a pet owner has booked an appointment for a given day, when the day before arrives, then the owner receives exactly one SMS reminder for it (R1).
- Given a reminder is sent, when the owner reads it, then it shows the salon name and the appointment date and time (R2).
- Given an appointment is moved to a new date, when the day before the new date arrives, then the owner receives a reminder with the new date and time, and none was sent for the old date (R3).
- Given an appointment has been cancelled, when the day before it would have been arrives, then no reminder is sent (R4).
- Given the gateway is selected, when its data processing is reviewed, then it is confirmed to process the owner's data in an EU region only (R5).
- Given a groomer has taken a booking and done nothing else, when the day before arrives, then the reminder is still sent (R6).

## Dependencies

- online-booking — reminders are based on the appointments that pet owners book and reschedule there, and on the phone number the owner gives when booking.
- SMS gateway — a third-party provider that processes data in an EU region. It is not yet chosen (hub assumption A5); choosing it is a design decision.

## Out of scope

- Reminders at times other than the day before the appointment.
- Channels other than SMS, such as email or app notifications.
- Replies from the pet owner, such as confirming or cancelling by text.
- Payments or deposits (see the deposits feature).

# Deposits at booking

## Summary

Deposits let a pet owner pay a deposit at the moment they book an appointment. A paid deposit gives the owner a reason to turn up and gives the groomer some protection when they do not, which helps cut the no-shows that cost groomers about a fifth of their slots. The deposit is part of the booking step in online booking; it is not a general payment service.

## Goals served

- G2 — Fewer no-shows: taking a deposit when the booking is made gives the pet owner a stake in the appointment, moving the no-show rate toward below 5% of appointments by 2027-06-30.

## Requirements

- **R1** — When a pet owner books an appointment, the booking flow asks for a deposit before the booking is confirmed.
- **R2** — The deposit amount is shown to the pet owner before they pay, and the pet owner must accept it to complete the booking.
- **R3** — A booking is confirmed only after the deposit payment has succeeded; if payment fails or is abandoned, the booking is not confirmed and the time is not held for that pet owner.
- **R4** — After a successful payment, the pet owner sees a confirmation that states the deposit paid, and the groomer can see that the deposit for that appointment has been paid.
- **R5** — The pet owner's payment details are handled only by the payment provider chosen at design time and are not stored by groomr.
- **R6** — All personal data handled for deposits is stored and processed in an EU region, in line with GDPR.

## Acceptance criteria

- Given a pet owner has chosen a free time and service, when they reach the last step of booking, then they are asked to pay a deposit before the booking is confirmed (R1).
- Given the deposit step is shown, when the pet owner views it, then the deposit amount is visible before any payment is made and the booking cannot be completed without accepting it (R2).
- Given a pet owner starts paying a deposit, when the payment fails or they leave the step, then no confirmed booking exists for that time and the pet owner is told the booking was not completed (R3).
- Given a deposit payment succeeds, when the booking is confirmed, then the pet owner sees the deposit amount paid on the confirmation and the groomer sees the appointment marked as deposit paid (R3, R4).
- Given any deposit payment, when the stored data of groomr is inspected, then it holds no card or other payment credentials entered by the pet owner (R5).
- Given deposit data is stored or processed, when its hosting location is checked, then it is in an EU region (R6).

## Dependencies

- online-booking — the deposit is taken inside the booking flow, so booking and its confirmation must exist first.
- Payment method and provider — not yet decided (assumption A3 in the hub); to be settled at design time. The choice must process data in the EU to meet the hub's EU data constraint.

## Out of scope

- Payments beyond deposits, as the hub states: paying for the full service, tips, product sales and any other charge.
- Choosing or naming the payment method or provider; this is left to design (A3).
- Rules for refunding or keeping a deposit when an appointment is cancelled or missed; not decided in the brief and left to design.

# Loyalty stamp card

## Summary

Repeat customers collect stamps toward a reward, which gives them a reason to come back to the same groomer and to book that next visit online. The feature answers a groomer's wish to keep regular customers and make return visits go through the online booking page rather than a phone call or text. The reward rules (how many stamps, what the reward is) are not yet decided (assumption A4 in the product PRD), so this document describes what the product must do with a rule, not what the rule is.

## Goals served

- G1 — Groomers take bookings online: a stamp earned on one online booking encourages the pet owner to make the next booking online, which adds to the weekly booking count.

## Requirements

- **R1** — The groomer can set up a stamp card for their salon, including the reward rules (number of stamps needed and the type of reward), and can change those rules later.
- **R2** — When a pet owner's appointment booked through groomr is completed, the pet owner receives one stamp on that salon's card.
- **R3** — The pet owner can see their current stamp count and what is needed for the reward when they book online.
- **R4** — When a pet owner reaches the number of stamps the groomer has set, the reward is marked as earned and is shown to both the pet owner and the groomer.
- **R5** — The groomer can mark an earned reward as redeemed, and a redeemed reward cannot be redeemed again.
- **R6** — A stamp card belongs to one salon; stamps earned at one salon do not count at another.
- **R7** — Stamp and reward data about a pet owner is stored and processed in an EU region, and the pet owner's stamp data can be deleted on request, in line with GDPR.

## Acceptance criteria

- Given a salon with a stamp card, when the groomer saves new reward rules, then the card shows those rules to pet owners from then on (R1).
- Given a pet owner with a completed online appointment at a salon with a stamp card, when the appointment is marked completed, then their stamp count at that salon goes up by one (R2).
- Given a pet owner with at least one stamp, when they open the booking page of that salon, then they see their stamp count and the stamps still needed for the reward (R3).
- Given a pet owner whose stamp count reaches the salon's required number, when the last stamp is added, then the reward is shown as earned to the pet owner and the groomer (R4).
- Given an earned reward, when the groomer marks it redeemed, then it shows as redeemed and cannot be marked redeemed a second time (R5).
- Given a pet owner with stamps at salon A, when they view salon B's card, then none of salon A's stamps are counted (R6).
- Given a pet owner's stamp data, when it is stored, then it sits in an EU region, and when the pet owner asks for deletion, then their stamp data is removed (R7).

## Dependencies

- online-booking — stamps are earned from appointments booked through the online booking page, and the stamp count is shown on that page.
- Decision on the loyalty reward rules (assumption A4 in the product PRD), which is left to design; the numbers are not set here.

## Out of scope

- Choosing the reward rules (number of stamps, type of reward); these are open.
- Payments, discounts applied automatically at checkout, or any payment handling beyond deposits.
- Stamps shared or compared across salons, or any marketplace ranking of groomers.
- Stamp cards for customers who do not book online.

7	# PRD — groomr
8	
9	## Vision
10	
11	Every independent dog groomer takes bookings online without phone tag. groomr gives a one- or two-person grooming salon a simple online booking page, automatic reminders and deposits, so pet owners book from their phone and the groomer spends the day grooming rather than answering calls and texts.
12	
13	## Problem statement
14	
15	Independent dog groomers lose hours every week to booking by phone and text: answering calls while their hands are busy, chasing replies and juggling the diary by hand. On top of that, no-shows cost them about a fifth of their slots, and an empty slot is income that cannot be recovered. Pet owners, for their part, have to wait for a reply before they know whether a time is free. (The "about a fifth" figure is the brief's own estimate, not measured data; see assumption A2.)
16	
17	## Target users & personas
18	
19	- **Groomer** — runs a one- or two-person salon. Sets opening hours and the services on offer. Wants a full diary without phone tag; is frustrated by interruptions during work and by clients who do not turn up.
20	- **Pet owner** — books and reschedules from a phone. Wants to see free times and book straight away; is frustrated by waiting for a reply and by forgetting appointments.
21	
22	## Goals & success metrics
23	
24	| Goal | Metric |
25	|---|---|
26	| G1 Groomers take bookings online | 500 bookings a week across all salons combined, by 2027-03-31 |
27	| G2 Fewer no-shows | No-show rate below 5% of appointments, by 2027-06-30 (from a baseline of about 20% of slots) |
28	
29	## Features (prioritized)
30	
31	### Must have
32	
33	- [Online booking](features/online-booking/prd.md) — pet owners book and reschedule appointments online against the groomer's opening hours and services (supports G1)
34	- [SMS reminders](features/sms-reminders/prd.md) — the pet owner receives an SMS reminder the day before the appointment (supports G2)
35	
36	### Should have
37	
38	- [Deposits at booking](features/deposits/prd.md) — the pet owner pays a deposit when booking, to reduce no-shows (supports G2)
39	
40	### Could have
41	
42	- [Loyalty stamp card](features/loyalty-stamp-card/prd.md) — repeat customers collect stamps toward a reward, encouraging return online bookings (supports G1)
43	
44	### Won't have
45	
46	- Marketplace ranking groomers against each other — groomr serves each salon's own customers and does not compare salons, which would work against the independent groomers it is built for.
47	
48	Both goals are served by at least one feature, so no goal is deferred.
49	
50	## Non-functional requirements
51	
52	- The booking page loads in under 2 seconds at p95 on a 4G phone.
53	- The service is available at least 99.5% of each month.
54	
55	## Constraints & assumptions
56	
57	Constraints:
58	
59	- Customers are in the EU only.
60	- All personal data is stored and processed in an EU region, in line with GDPR.
61	- SMS messages are sent through a third-party gateway.
62	
63	Assumptions (to be confirmed or replaced as the product is designed):
64	
65	- **A1** — The 500 bookings a week in G1 is the total across all salons combined, as the brief states.
66	- **A2** — The baseline no-show rate of about 20% is the brief's "about a fifth of their slots", an estimate rather than measured data.
67	- **A3** — The deposit payment method and provider are not yet decided; they are left to design.
68	- **A4** — The loyalty reward rules (number of stamps, type of reward) are not yet decided; they are left to design.
69	- **A5** — The SMS gateway is not yet chosen; it must process data in the EU to meet the data constraint above.
70	
71	## Out of scope
72	
73	- Native mobile apps; booking is through the web on a phone.
74	- Payments beyond deposits.
75	- Marketplace ranking of groomers against each other.
76

6	
7	# Online booking
8	
9	## Summary
10	
11	Online booking lets a pet owner book and reschedule a grooming appointment from their phone, choosing from the times a groomer has actually left open. The groomer sets their opening hours and the services they offer, and the booking page works from those. This removes the phone and text back-and-forth that costs independent groomers hours every week, and lets pet owners see a free time and book it straight away.
12	
13	## Goals served
14	
15	- G1 — Groomers take bookings online: this feature is how a booking is made, so every booking counted toward the 500 a week by 2027-03-31 goes through it.
16	
17	## Requirements
18	
19	- **R1** — A groomer can set their opening hours.
20	- **R2** — A groomer can set the services they offer.
21	- **R3** — A pet owner can see the times that are free, based on the groomer's opening hours, the services offered and appointments already booked.
22	- **R4** — A pet owner can book an appointment for a chosen service in a free time, from a phone browser, without calling or texting the groomer.
23	- **R5** — A pet owner can reschedule an existing appointment to another free time, from a phone browser.
24	- **R6** — The same time cannot be booked twice for the same groomer.
25	- **R7** — The booking page loads in under 2 seconds at p95 on a 4G phone connection.
26	- **R8** — All personal data collected through booking is stored and processed in an EU region.
27	
28	## Acceptance criteria
29	
30	- Given a groomer has set opening hours and services, when a pet owner opens the booking page, then only times inside those hours, for those services, and not already booked are offered (R1, R2, R3).
31	- Given a free time is offered, when a pet owner books it on a phone, then the appointment is confirmed and appears in the groomer's diary without any call or text (R4).
32	- Given a pet owner has an appointment, when they reschedule it to another free time on a phone, then the new time is held for them and the old time is offered as free again (R5).
33	- Given two pet owners try to book the same time for the same groomer, when both submit, then only one booking succeeds and the other is told the time is taken (R6).
34	- Given page-load measurements of the booking page on a 4G phone connection, when the p95 is calculated over a month, then it is under 2 seconds (R7).
35	- Given the hosting and storage configuration, when it is inspected, then every store and service that holds booking personal data is in an EU region (R8).
36	
37	## Dependencies
38	
39	None.
40	
41	## Out of scope
42	
43	- Deposits taken at booking (see the deposits feature).
44	- SMS reminders (see the sms-reminders feature).
45	- Loyalty stamps (see the loyalty-stamp-card feature).
46	- Native mobile apps; booking is through the web on a phone.
47

6	
7	# SMS reminders
8	
9	## Summary
10	
11	The pet owner gets a text message the day before their grooming appointment. Owners forget appointments, and every no-show leaves the groomer with an empty slot that cannot be recovered. A reminder sent without any effort from the groomer helps owners turn up, or tell the groomer in good time. The messages go out through a third-party SMS gateway that must process data in an EU region.
12	
13	## Goals served
14	
15	- G2 — Fewer no-shows. Reminding the owner the day before the appointment is aimed at bringing the no-show rate below 5% of appointments by 2027-06-30, from a baseline of about 20%.
16	
17	## Requirements
18	
19	- **R1** — For every booked appointment, the pet owner receives one SMS reminder on the day before the appointment.
20	- **R2** — The reminder names the salon and gives the date and time of the appointment.
21	- **R3** — If an appointment is rescheduled, the reminder follows the new date and time, and no reminder is sent for the old one.
22	- **R4** — If an appointment is cancelled, no reminder is sent for it.
23	- **R5** — Reminders are sent through a third-party SMS gateway that processes data in an EU region only (constraint in the hub; assumption A5, the gateway is not yet chosen).
24	- **R6** — The groomer does not have to do anything for reminders to be sent.
25	
26	## Acceptance criteria
27	
28	- Given a pet owner has booked an appointment for a given day, when the day before arrives, then the owner receives exactly one SMS reminder for it (R1).
29	- Given a reminder is sent, when the owner reads it, then it shows the salon name and the appointment date and time (R2).
30	- Given an appointment is moved to a new date, when the day before the new date arrives, then the owner receives a reminder with the new date and time, and none was sent for the old date (R3).
31	- Given an appointment has been cancelled, when the day before it would have been arrives, then no reminder is sent (R4).
32	- Given the gateway is selected, when its data processing is reviewed, then it is confirmed to process the owner's data in an EU region only (R5).
33	- Given a groomer has taken a booking and done nothing else, when the day before arrives, then the reminder is still sent (R6).
34	
35	## Dependencies
36	
37	- online-booking — reminders are based on the appointments that pet owners book and reschedule there, and on the phone number the owner gives when booking.
38	- SMS gateway — a third-party provider that processes data in an EU region. It is not yet chosen (hub assumption A5); choosing it is a design decision.
39	
40	## Out of scope
41	
42	- Reminders at times other than the day before the appointment.
43	- Channels other than SMS, such as email or app notifications.
44	- Replies from the pet owner, such as confirming or cancelling by text.
45	- Payments or deposits (see the deposits feature).
46

6	
7	# Deposits at booking
8	
9	## Summary
10	
11	Deposits let a pet owner pay a deposit at the moment they book an appointment. A paid deposit gives the owner a reason to turn up and gives the groomer some protection when they do not, which helps cut the no-shows that cost groomers about a fifth of their slots. The deposit is part of the booking step in online booking; it is not a general payment service.
12	
13	## Goals served
14	
15	- G2 — Fewer no-shows: taking a deposit when the booking is made gives the pet owner a stake in the appointment, moving the no-show rate toward below 5% of appointments by 2027-06-30.
16	
17	## Requirements
18	
19	- **R1** — When a pet owner books an appointment, the booking flow asks for a deposit before the booking is confirmed.
20	- **R2** — The deposit amount is shown to the pet owner before they pay, and the pet owner must accept it to complete the booking.
21	- **R3** — A booking is confirmed only after the deposit payment has succeeded; if payment fails or is abandoned, the booking is not confirmed and the time is not held for that pet owner.
22	- **R4** — After a successful payment, the pet owner sees a confirmation that states the deposit paid, and the groomer can see that the deposit for that appointment has been paid.
23	- **R5** — The pet owner's payment details are handled only by the payment provider chosen at design time and are not stored by groomr.
24	- **R6** — All personal data handled for deposits is stored and processed in an EU region, in line with GDPR.
25	
26	## Acceptance criteria
27	
28	- Given a pet owner has chosen a free time and service, when they reach the last step of booking, then they are asked to pay a deposit before the booking is confirmed (R1).
29	- Given the deposit step is shown, when the pet owner views it, then the deposit amount is visible before any payment is made and the booking cannot be completed without accepting it (R2).
30	- Given a pet owner starts paying a deposit, when the payment fails or they leave the step, then no confirmed booking exists for that time and the pet owner is told the booking was not completed (R3).
31	- Given a deposit payment succeeds, when the booking is confirmed, then the pet owner sees the deposit amount paid on the confirmation and the groomer sees the appointment marked as deposit paid (R3, R4).
32	- Given any deposit payment, when the stored data of groomr is inspected, then it holds no card or other payment credentials entered by the pet owner (R5).
33	- Given deposit data is stored or processed, when its hosting location is checked, then it is in an EU region (R6).
34	
35	## Dependencies
36	
37	- online-booking — the deposit is taken inside the booking flow, so booking and its confirmation must exist first.
38	- Payment method and provider — not yet decided (assumption A3 in the hub); to be settled at design time. The choice must process data in the EU to meet the hub's EU data constraint.
39	
40	## Out of scope
41	
42	- Payments beyond deposits, as the hub states: paying for the full service, tips, product sales and any other charge.
43	- Choosing or naming the payment method or provider; this is left to design (A3).
44	- Rules for refunding or keeping a deposit when an appointment is cancelled or missed; not decided in the brief and left to design.
45

2	status: "proposed"
3	version: 1
4	tickets: []
5	---
6	
7	# Loyalty stamp card
8	
9	## Summary
10	
11	Repeat customers collect stamps toward a reward, which gives them a reason to come back to the same groomer and to book that next visit online. The feature answers a groomer's wish to keep regular customers and make return visits go through the online booking page rather than a phone call or text. The reward rules (how many stamps, what the reward is) are not yet decided (assumption A4 in the product PRD), so this document describes what the product must do with a rule, not what the rule is.
12	
13	## Goals served
14	
15	- G1 — Groomers take bookings online: a stamp earned on one online booking encourages the pet owner to make the next booking online, which adds to the weekly booking count.
16	
17	## Requirements
18	
19	- **R1** — The groomer can set up a stamp card for their salon, including the reward rules (number of stamps needed and the type of reward), and can change those rules later.
20	- **R2** — When a pet owner's appointment booked through groomr is completed, the pet owner receives one stamp on that salon's card.
21	- **R3** — The pet owner can see their current stamp count and what is needed for the reward when they book online.
22	- **R4** — When a pet owner reaches the number of stamps the groomer has set, the reward is marked as earned and is shown to both the pet owner and the groomer.
23	- **R5** — The groomer can mark an earned reward as redeemed, and a redeemed reward cannot be redeemed again.
24	- **R6** — A stamp card belongs to one salon; stamps earned at one salon do not count at another.
25	- **R7** — Stamp and reward data about a pet owner is stored and processed in an EU region, and the pet owner's stamp data can be deleted on request, in line with GDPR.
26	
27	## Acceptance criteria
28	
29	- Given a salon with a stamp card, when the groomer saves new reward rules, then the card shows those rules to pet owners from then on (R1).
30	- Given a pet owner with a completed online appointment at a salon with a stamp card, when the appointment is marked completed, then their stamp count at that salon goes up by one (R2).
31	- Given a pet owner with at least one stamp, when they open the booking page of that salon, then they see their stamp count and the stamps still needed for the reward (R3).
32	- Given a pet owner whose stamp count reaches the salon's required number, when the last stamp is added, then the reward is shown as earned to the pet owner and the groomer (R4).
33	- Given an earned reward, when the groomer marks it redeemed, then it shows as redeemed and cannot be marked redeemed a second time (R5).
34	- Given a pet owner with stamps at salon A, when they view salon B's card, then none of salon A's stamps are counted (R6).
35	- Given a pet owner's stamp data, when it is stored, then it sits in an EU region, and when the pet owner asks for deletion, then their stamp data is removed (R7).
36	
37	## Dependencies
38	
39	- online-booking — stamps are earned from appointments booked through the online booking page, and the stamp count is shown on that page.
40	- Decision on the loyalty reward rules (assumption A4 in the product PRD), which is left to design; the numbers are not set here.
41	
42	## Out of scope
43	
44	- Choosing the reward rules (number of stamps, type of reward); these are open.
45	- Payments, discounts applied automatically at checkout, or any payment handling beyond deposits.
46	- Stamps shared or compared across salons, or any marketplace ranking of groomers.
47	- Stamp cards for customers who do not book online.
48

# SMS reminders

## Summary

The pet owner gets a text message the day before their grooming appointment. Owners forget appointments, and every no-show leaves the groomer with an empty slot that cannot be recovered. A reminder sent without any effort from the groomer helps owners turn up, or tell the groomer in good time. The messages go out through a third-party SMS gateway that must process data in an EU region.

## Goals served

- G2 — Fewer no-shows. Reminding the owner the day before the appointment is aimed at bringing the no-show rate below 5% of appointments by 2027-06-30, from a baseline of about 20%.

## Requirements

- **R1** — For every booked appointment, the pet owner receives one SMS reminder on the day before the appointment.
- **R2** — The reminder names the salon and gives the date and time of the appointment.
- **R3** — If an appointment is rescheduled, the reminder follows the new date and time, and no reminder is sent for the old one.
- **R4** — If an appointment is cancelled, no reminder is sent for it.
- **R5** — Reminders are sent through a third-party SMS gateway that processes data in an EU region only (constraint in the hub; assumption A5, the gateway is not yet chosen).
- **R6** — The groomer does not have to do anything for reminders to be sent.

## Acceptance criteria

- Given a pet owner has booked an appointment for a given day, when the day before arrives, then the owner receives exactly one SMS reminder for it (R1).
- Given a reminder is sent, when the owner reads it, then it shows the salon name and the appointment date and time (R2).
- Given an appointment is moved to a new date, when the day before the new date arrives, then the owner receives a reminder with the new date and time, and none was sent for the old date (R3).
- Given an appointment has been cancelled, when the day before it would have been arrives, then no reminder is sent (R4).
- Given the gateway is selected, when its data processing is reviewed, then it is confirmed to process the owner's data in an EU region only (R5).
- Given a groomer has taken a booking and done nothing else, when the day before arrives, then the reminder is still sent (R6).

## Dependencies

- online-booking — reminders are based on the appointments that pet owners book and reschedule there, and on the phone number the owner gives when booking.
- SMS gateway — a third-party provider that processes data in an EU region. It is not yet chosen (hub assumption A5); choosing it is a design decision.

## Out of scope

- Reminders at times other than the day before the appointment.
- Channels other than SMS, such as email or app notifications.
- Replies from the pet owner, such as confirming or cancelling by text.
- Payments or deposits (see the deposits feature).
